steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Consonant harmony sounds stable and restful; dissonant harmony sounds tense and unresolved — both are deliberate compositional choices.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Cadences are harmonic endings: perfect (V-I, final), plagal (IV-I, amen), imperfect (I-V or IV-V, unfinished), interrupted (V-vi, surprise).

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Modulation changes the key centre: to the dominant (5th scale degree), subdominant (4th), or relative major/minor — each creates a different shift of mood.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Pedal notes are sustained or repeated while harmony changes above them — dominant pedals build tension; tonic pedals create stability.

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Describe how harmony and tonality are used in a piece of music you have studied. Use musical vocabulary. | Compare how two different pieces use harmony and tonality. Explain the effect in each case. | How could you use harmony and tonality in your own composition or performance? Explain your choices.

steps.title: Check your answers
steps.body: A detailed description using precise musical vocabulary (e.g. specific terms from the AQA elements list), referencing a named piece with accurate observations about how the elements are used and their | A comparison of two pieces identifying similarities and differences in how harmony and tonality are used, explaining the different effects created in each musical context, using comparative language. | A practical application showing understanding of how harmony and tonality can be manipulated in composition or performance, with specific examples of choices made and their intended effect.

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Always use PRECISE musical vocabulary — not vague descriptions like it sounds nice Reference SPECIFIC musical elements when analysing any piece For listening questions: identify elements FIRST, then explain their effect For study pieces: know the context, structure and key features in detail For performing: focus on accuracy, expression and interpretation For composing: show development of ideas, not just repetition
